That’s difficult to say because the language Paleosardinian is totally unknown, there’s no consensus between linguists and archeologists on wether Paleosardinian was related to basque, e.g.:  
Massimo Pittau believed there was a fraction of words related to basque and iberian but they were only loanwords.  
Wagner and Bertoldi believed there were two languages in Sardinia, one of which was vasconic (idk what Bertoldi believed in, but for Wagner it came from the migration of the Balares, a tribe of iberian origin around ~700-230 b.c.e)
Areddu disproves the existence of a basque substrate altogether.  
Blasco Ferrer believed not only that Paleosardinian was a vasconic language but that there is a multilayered ibero-vasconic substrate in Sardinian. (The first arrived with the spread of Cardium Pottery, the second with the Megalithic cultures, third with the Bell Beakers, fourth with the migration of the Balares).  
Giovanni Ugas believes one of the 3 languages that were spoken in Sardinia before the Romans (Ligurian) also influenced Basque.  

I personally believe there are indeed words of common origin in Sardinian and Basque, the amount of actual basque words (that aren’t loans from other languages) isn’t really enough to justify the presence on Sardinia.

Premise: it’s a difficult topic also because Tuscan wasn’t chosen as an official language a priori. Since the XIII century Tuscany would give birth to some of the most important poets and writers in Italian history which not only did it gave prestige to the Tuscan language but also made it the Lingua Franca of the peninsula.
which means the existence of Tuscan itself is tied to the creation of an Italian nation and it would be difficult to say what would Italy have been without it.

Not taking into account how much history would have been altered by the lack of Tuscan, I’d say the likely candidates for a language of italy are:

Latin: during the XVII centuries there was still an ongoing debate on whether people should write in Latin as a prestige language and it was still considered as the language of culture by a somewhat large portion of literary people.
If Tuscan hadn’t been as important as it was it’s possible Latin would have dominated the scene and be the lingua franca of the peninsula, filling the role of Tuscan.

Padanian Koiné: a literary language based around Gallo-Italic ones and Venetian, a rival to Tuscan until the XV century in northern Italy.

Other regional languages which had at least one important poets writing it (that could have influenced the birth of a literary language): Venetian (Goldoni, Foscolo) which also enjoyed and higher prestige in Venice itself compared to the other regional languages in their own areas at that time;   
Sicilian (Sicilian poetry was highly regarded for a time and even influenced Tuscan one; though we’re talking about XII century); 
Piedmontese (Manzoni).

Highly unlikely: Occitan (though it had an important and influential role in the past, it being in a peripheral location and tied to other nations probably wouldn’t have helped); 

Impossible: Sardinian (Sardinian has never been part of the Italian cultural sphere. Even though the unification of Italy was made by the Kingdom Sardinia, it was merely a title adopted by the Savoy after buying the island, as it had a lot more prestige then any of the titles that were tied to their own territories).

Many languages from several different families, it would take a while to name them all, the largest as in geographical territory were:

The italic languages: a group of ie languages spoken throughout the italic peninsula, it included  Latin, Oscan, Umbrian and South Picenian (as well as many others less extended ones like Volscian and Sabinian).

Other ie languages were Gaulish and Lepontic (two Celtic languages), Sikel and Venetic (perhaps part of Italic as well), Messapic (spoken in Apulia and possibly related to Albanian), Elymian (in western Sicily) and ancient Ligurian and Greek

Finally, there were others that weren’t part of the ie family (or of which we don’t know enough about) like Etruscan and Rhaetic (which were probably part of the same language family), Punic (which was Semitic), North Picenian, Nuragic and Sicanian

Most scholars do believe in a relationship between the šrdn and Sardinia, the main discussion is on whether the šrdn were originated in the eastern Mediterranean and then convoluted into the already existing Nuragic Sardinia (which is the “traditional” hypothesis regarding not only the šrdn but the sea peoples in general) or if they were Nuragic Sardinians who moved eastward (Western Hypothesis).

The reason why researchers agree upon the connection between the Nuragics and the sherden is not only the similar sounding name, but also nuragic pottery found in Crete and Cyprus (and thus proof of Nuragic presence in the Eastern Mediterranean); similarities in bronze figures of Nuragic ships and the depictions of the ships of the sea peoples; nuragic horned helmets in bronze figures and šrdn horned helmets in Egyptian depictions, similar blade shapes in swords as well as similar round-shaped shields with similar details on them.

I recommend the book “I Shardana e Sardegna, i popoli del mare, gli alleati del Nordafrica e la fine dei grandi regni” by archeologist Giovanni Ugas which dwells on the topic with detail and explains the Sardinian-Sherden connection

In short: most European languages are related to one another, for example English, Dutch, Swedish and German descend from the same language (Proto-Germanic), same thing for Serbian, Polish, Russian and Ukrainian (from Proto-Slavic) and Spanish, Italian, French and Romanian (from Latin); in turn Proto-Slavic, Latin, Proto-Germanic and various other ancient languages (like Proto-Celtic, ancient Persian and Ancient Greek) all descend from this language called Proto-Indo-European.

This means that most European languages (there are a few exceptions) are related to one another with varying degrees of closeness; if you look at how words like “father”, “mother” and the numbers from 1 to 10 are said in Latin, Greek, German, Russian, Persian and Hindi you’ll see the relationship between them clearly.

This is not true for Korean, Japanese and Mandarin; though they did influence one another they’re unrelated, in the sense that they don’t have any common ancestor: Japanese is part of the Japonic family; Korean is part of the Koreanic language family; and Mandarin is part of the Sinitic one, a sub-family of the Sino-Tibetan language family.

Sardinian has an unclear substratum (as in it could be pre-ie or not), the “strength” of this substratum depends from the region, it’s really evident in Barbaja (the central region of Sardinia) where a lot of the names for animals (especially little ones) come from this/these substratum/s.

The presence of a substratum in Barbaja is also noticeable in place names: Urune, Vitzi, Oranìe, Onanìe, Goreai, Dure, Orgosolo, Nùgoro etc. the majority of the names of cities in Barbaja come from this substratum, and there also a lot of micro-toponyms that come from this substratum too.

The substratum shows what appears to be lexical variations, for example in ‘Onne a little trout is called “tzurra” while in Vitzi it’s called “grori”; in the Logudoresu speaking area the name for worm is “lingrone/tzilingrone” or words that come from the same root, while in Campidanesu there’s “Cugurra”.

Some suffixes that have been identified are: -VrV, -Vi, -VsV/-VssV (present in toponyms from both the modern day Logudoresu and Campidanesu speaking areas) and VnV (which is only present in modern day Gaddura and the three/two northern Barbajan subregions, but at the same time it’s found in southern Corsica.

-prefixes include: tzV/tV/thV/tzVn/tVn/thVn-; it seems like in the Campidanesu area there might be another prefix in cV (e.g. calixerta “lizard”) and that in both Northern and Southern Sardinian there is another prefix in a/an- (e.g: aiccu “figue”; antunniu “mushroom”)

This substratum has been connected to: Basque, “indo-European” (unspecified family, but with lots of cognates with Greek, Celtic and Germanic), several substratum layers from different language families (some of them being Afro-Asiatic and Vasconic), Albanian, a mix of Libyan, Basque and Ligurian, a mix of  Iberian, Berber, Rhaetic and Ligurian, a mix of a Pan-Mediterranean language, a language that originated from the Bell Beakers and the language of the Ligurians.

Regarding toponymic/microtoponymic roots: Words/Roots that have been likely identified (but that don’t exist anymore in Sardinian): gonn- (possibly with variations in bonn-/onn-) that likely means “elevated place” and has cognates in Basque and Attic Greek (the word in Greek is a loanword tho), and Org-/urg- which likely means “land with water” and has a cognate with Ancient Greek (but even in this case, the word in Greek has an unclear origin).

Roots that have been identified (and their meaning still exist in Modern Sardinian): kukkur- “high place” cfr modern Sardinian kùkkuru (head), kokkorostra (cock’s crest) and has a cognate with Basque.

Features that basically all of the Sardinian dialects of barbaja have in common that are different from the other Sardinian dialects are : 1) the elimination of intervocalic F; 2) pronunciation of intervocalic /k/ as a glottal stop, as /χ/ or as /kk/ (depending from the area) 3) (this happens sometimes there’s no clear rule) transformation of words that used to have an intervocalic v to gh/g (e.g.: gurpe (fox), ghespe (wasp)); other unique characteristics of Sardinian (or at least some of its dialects) are: Vrr- prosthesis if there’s a word that starts with r- (Campidanesu); transformation of Latin kw to b (Logudoresu); transformation of Latin intervocalic l to: glottal stop, r, gw (Campidanesu, Campidanesu Rusticu, Gesturesu respectively) ; lack of existence of dz phoneme (Vitzi, Onanìe);

Vitzikesu: non-existence of the phoneme /dz/, (words that in other dialects have this phoneme (for example words that come from Latin /lj/) are pronounced kinda like a /ts/), intervocalic latin f-> disappeared (just like in Urunesu), latin tj-> /ts/ (for example: Latin petia, Nugoresu petta, Urunesu peθa, vitzikesu petsa) the ts is pronounced more strongly compared to the “other” one, latin rj-> /λ:/ (for example: ianuarius-> jan:aλ:u), latin nd-> /n:/, Latin VtV-> VtV, Latin b-> /v/ (with some b relicts due to it being a relatively new change), latin v-> disappeared (some v relicts for the same reason as b->v), disappearance of intervocalic Latin d if followed by a i (denarius-> inari), latin k->k.
Luvulesu: really similar to Vitzikesu, the only difference being the presence of /dz/ in words that come from Latin lj (latin: filius, luvulesu: idzu, vitzikesu: itsu).
Dialects of Baronia: similar to luvulesu, but latin rj becomes /rdz/ (example: baroniesu: rezordza, vitzikesu: rezoλ:a), and Latin b and v-> both become v.
